title: Meet the liburna:
the fast raiding galley of the Liburnians, an Illyrian seafaring people of the eastern Adriatic.
anatomy: The early form, from the sixth and fifth centuries BC, is known from a carving on the Novilara stele.
It has a prow that curves outward,
one mast with a single square sail,
and a single bank of oars, twenty-five on each side.
A steering oar sits at the stern.
The hull is light, low and open: built for speed.
sewn: Liburnian boatbuilders sewed their hulls together.
Thin planks, about one and a half to two centimetres thick,
were laced with cord of flax and Spanish broom.
Small wooden pegs locked every stitch, about every two and a half centimetres.
We know this from boats found at Zaton and Tsaska. Whether the war galleys were sewn the same way is not known.
oars: Each rower needs about a metre of hull.
Twenty-five in a row means roughly twenty-five metres of benches alone.
A long, narrow hull is fast in a straight line, but slow to turn.
bireme: In the first century BC, Rome adopted the design
and stacked the rowers on two levels.
The later Roman form had eighteen oars per side, in two rows.
Same muscle, shorter hull, quicker turns.
A deck and protection from missiles were added.
One modern reconstruction gives it fifty oars, and eighteen by three metres at the waterline.
ram: The main weapon is the bronze ram at the bow.
It strikes the enemy hull below the waterline,
and the sea does the rest.
outro: More than seven knots under oars,
and a key role at the Battle of Actium in thirty-one BC.
Small, light and quick, the liburna became the core of Rome's provincial fleets.
